title: Visual Representation Learning for Preference-Aware Path Planning
reading_depth: Full main text, PDF pp. 1–6, plus visual inspection of PDF p. 5 to verify Table I and the printed metric equation. References not close-read; metric implementation not inspected.
problem: Geometric free space does not encode terrain preferences, while fixed semantic classes require dense labels and handle hybrid terrain poorly.
mechanism: Mine same-location views and avoided shortcuts from demonstrations, learn a contrastive terrain embedding and relative preference costs, then augment a geometric local planner.
evidence_scope: Physical Jackal trials: 17 short primary-environment demonstrations, additional park demonstrations, a novel-gravel adaptation test, and a 440 m extended route.
writing_move: Connect each representation requirement to a training-pair construction, and show adaptation before and after additional demonstrations.
research_lesson: An annotation-saving method should expose the assumptions that make implicit labels valid, not equate unlabeled data with unconstrained data.
reviewer_question: How often do detours reflect terrain preference rather than another intention, and which exact distance computation and sampling normalization produced the reported path errors?

evidence_pages.observation: Straight demonstrations add no triplets, and suboptimal homogeneous-terrain demonstrations can create wrong labels; costs are relative, not identified absolutely.
Rendered Eq. 11 uses a sum of nearest-point distances despite the Hausdorff label; baseline path errors include manual intervention.
The initial model fails on novel gravel; three new demonstrations totaling 27 seconds enable adaptation. The extended route is one deployment example.

limits_or_counterexample: Novel-terrain adaptation includes new data and retraining, not zero-shot recognition. The printed metric discrepancy calls for code clarification, not a claim that the implementation is wrong; zero interventions on these routes is not general safety.
citation: Kavan Singh Sikand, Sadegh Rabiee, Adam Uccello, Xuesu Xiao , Garrett Warnell, and Joydeep Biswas. Visual Representation Learning for Preference-Aware Path Planning . 2022 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA).
venue_full: 2022 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)

title: Machine Learning Methods for Local Motion Planning: A Study of End-to-End vs. Parameter Learning
reading_depth: Full main text, PDF pp. 1–6, including task/reward definitions, matched architecture choices, simulated/physical results, and conclusion. References not close-read; no code or statistical replication.
problem: Common beliefs about end-to-end versus planner-parameter learning lacked controlled navigation comparisons.
mechanism: Train TD3 policies over direct velocities or DWA parameters, vary observation representation and training-environment count, and test on held-out environments and a physical Jackal.
evidence_scope: BARN: 50 held-out environments; training sets of 10, 50, or 250; twenty evaluation trials per environment. Physical tests use three trials per method in each of three settings.
writing_move: Turn a paradigm debate into explicit factors, shared infrastructure, held-out performance, and a multi-metric comparison.
research_lesson: Use train/test contrast to expose overfitting, while disclosing nonidentical reward and control-frequency choices rather than claiming a universally decisive comparison.
reviewer_question: Are conclusions robust to tuning budgets and controller frequencies, and do the chosen proxy metrics support the intended safety and smoothness claims?

evidence_pages.observation: The parameter policy omits the collision-penalty term and updates every second; direct control updates every 0.2 seconds.
'Collisions' are proximity-defined soft collisions, traversal time conditions on success, and 'smoothness' is the fraction of positive linear commands.
End-to-end costmap results are omitted from plots due to poor learning, with a latency hypothesis; physical comparisons use only three trials per setting.
The conclusion explicitly leaves sensitivity to manually selected training/reward hyperparameters for future investigation.

limits_or_counterexample: The tested parameter policies generalize better, but neither these metrics nor DWA ancestry alone prove unrestricted safety or universal superiority over all end-to-end designs.
citation: Zifan Xu, Xuesu Xiao , Garrett Warnell, Anirudh Nair, and Peter Stone. Machine Learning Methods for Local Motion Planning: A Study of End-to-End vs. Parameter Learning . 2021 IEEE International Symposium on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics (SSRR).
venue_full: 2021 IEEE International Symposium on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics (SSRR)

title: From Agile Ground to Aerial Navigation: Learning from Learned Hallucination
reading_depth: Full main text, PDF pp. 1–6, including ground/aerial implementations and limitations; PDF p. 6 Table III visually verified. References not close-read; no code or optimality proof replication.
problem: Handcrafted hallucination rules restrict robot morphology and training-plan horizons.
mechanism: Learn obstacle distributions with an encoder and fixed differentiable planner decoder, reconstruct observed plans, then train a policy on sampled and rendered obstacle scenes.
evidence_scope: Ground: 300 BARN environments, three trials per condition, and five physical-course trials per planner. Quantified aerial evaluation uses ten simulated forest runs; ground/aerial models and data pipelines differ.
writing_move: Identify the predecessor's approximation boundary, learn the formerly handcrafted operation, and test a distinct embodiment.
research_lesson: Separate a general framework from the concrete data-generating policy and deployment checks; retain trade-offs rather than summarize every metric as a win.
reviewer_question: Does performance survive genuinely random aerial exploration and ablation of collision checking, and how much quality comes from the fixed planner used during learning?

evidence_pages.observation: Ground hallucinations use tuned priors, clearance filtering, extra obstacles, and MPC collision checking during deployment.
Aerial training uses twenty minutes of Ego-Planner trajectories in constrained simulation with perception discarded; truly random open-space aerial exploration is explicitly future work.
Visually verified: LfLH survives longer but SPL is 0.56 versus Ego-Planner's 0.74. Aerial collision checking remains part of the system.

limits_or_counterexample: The UAV experiment is not a direct realization of the random-open-space data story. Reported survival gains trade off path efficiency; simulated survival and qualitative physical references do not provide a general aerial safety guarantee.
citation: Zizhao Wang, Xuesu Xiao , Alexander J Nettekoven, Kadhiravan Umasankar, Anika Singh, Sriram Bommakanti, Ufuk Topcu, and Peter Stone. From Agile Ground to Aerial Navigation: Learning from Learned Hallucination . 2021 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS).
venue_full: 2021 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)

title: Team Orienteering Coverage Planning with Uncertain Reward
reading_depth: Full main text, PDF pp. 1–6, including formulation, proposition/proof, algorithms, counterexample, results, and physical-demo scope. Proof read for argument, not independently verified; references not close-read.
problem: Repeated fleet servicing must handle accumulating unknown costs and routes that revisit vertices, which standard TOP constraints do not capture.
mechanism: Estimate location-specific growth rates from visits and solve a new per-iteration mixed-integer coverage problem with repeated vertices and optional mandatory visits.
evidence_scope: 600 randomly generated small graph instances, comparing TOCP, TOP, and greedy planning under a solver time limit. The three-robot physical demonstration uses one iteration with known rewards.
writing_move: Explain why a seemingly small route constraint changes the mathematical problem, then disclose an explicit counterexample to horizon-wide optimality.
research_lesson: Distinguish exact solution of an inner optimization from optimality of the complete sequential policy, and separately report solver failures.
reviewer_question: How do runtime failures, reward nonstationarity, and paired-instance analysis change the comparison, and what evidence tests online uncertainty estimation on hardware?

evidence_pages.observation: Graphs are symmetric directed with equal reverse-edge lengths; this assumption supports the no-repeated-directed-edge proposition.
The authors identify decomposition and estimation suboptimality and construct a case where per-iteration optimization loses over the horizon.
Cost/time averages include only graphs where every method finds a solution, with a 1,000-second per-iteration limit; failures are reported separately.
The hardware demo fixes H=1 and supplies ground-truth rewards, so it does not demonstrate uncertain multi-iteration reward learning.

limits_or_counterexample: TOCP is not globally optimal TOCPUR. Hardware route feasibility is narrower than validation of the uncertainty model; dynamic collision avoidance lies outside the high-level formulation.
citation: Bo Liu, Xuesu Xiao , and Peter Stone. Team Orienteering Coverage Planning with Uncertain Reward . 2021 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS).
venue_full: 2021 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)

title: Agile Robot Navigation through Hallucinated Learning and Sober Deployment
reading_depth: Full main text, PDF pp. 1–6, including the point-robot propositions, practical approximation, sampling algorithm, recovery implementation, and experiments. Proofs read for argument, not independently verified; references not close-read.
problem: Earlier hallucination learning needs a fine global path and runtime perceptual transformation, and constant constrained observations make varying speeds ambiguous.
mechanism: Approximate a representative minimal obstacle set, sample additional plausible LiDAR scenes with speed-dependent clearance offsets, and train a policy that consumes real observations at deployment.
evidence_scope: 12,585 raw samples from 505 seconds of simulated open-space motion; 4,500 BARN evaluation trials and five physical-course trials per planner.
writing_move: Move from an intuitive geometric example and necessary conditions to a clearly labeled practical approximation, then compare both learning rule and training-speed distribution.
research_lesson: Explain exactly which dependency is removed and which protective engineering remains; test a failure-producing predecessor configuration as well as strong working baselines.
reviewer_question: When does the single-minimal-set approximation fail as horizon, speed, or geometry changes, and how much reported performance relies on collision checks and recovery?

evidence_pages.observation: Representing all minimal sets by one is explicitly a hypothesis justified empirically, especially for close configurations and discrete beams—not a proven equivalence.
The learned policy uses a one-action horizon and clipped 1 m scans; MPC collision checking triggers alignment and backing-up recovery.
Crossed speed-data conditions expose LfH label ambiguity; the conclusion specifies the safety guarantee during obstacle-free training.

limits_or_counterexample: Sober means no runtime hallucination, not an unguarded policy-only navigation stack. The point-robot propositions do not guarantee arbitrary nonholonomic deployment safety, and the short-horizon approximation limits extrapolation.
citation: Xuesu Xiao , Bo Liu, and Peter Stone. Agile Robot Navigation through Hallucinated Learning and Sober Deployment . 2021 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA).
venue_full: 2021 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)

title: APPLI: Adaptive Planner Parameter Learning from Interventions
reading_depth: Full main text, PDF pp. 1–6, including intervention protocol, confidence mechanism, physical tests, simulation ablations, and future work. References not close-read; no calibration or statistical reanalysis.
problem: Global retuning can damage already-good behavior; sparse corrective demonstrations can target failures and inefficiencies.
mechanism: Fit a planner-parameter set to each intervention, classify context with evidential confidence and temporal smoothing, and revert to default parameters when confidence is low.
evidence_scope: Four author-provided interventions; five physical trials per variant in each of two courses. Seven variants receive twelve runs in each of 300 simulated environments, totaling 25,200 evaluations.
writing_move: Distinguish necessary rescue interventions from optional efficiency corrections and cross intervention coverage with confidence ablations.
research_lesson: Preserving an adequate baseline and selectively learning from mistakes can outperform indiscriminate imitation, but this depends on demonstration quality and detection reliability.
reviewer_question: How well calibrated is confidence on genuinely unfamiliar failure states, and what changes when users cannot rewind the robot before demonstrating a correction?

evidence_pages.observation: Interventions reset the robot to where the problem began; Type A rescues failure while Type B improves suboptimal behavior.
One author supplies demonstrations; conservative full demonstrations can teach slower behavior than the already-adequate default. Physical stuck trials receive a 200-second penalty.
Confidence is important for two rescue contexts but removing it makes little difference with richer intervention coverage. Non-rewinding interventions remain future work.

limits_or_counterexample: A low-confidence fallback is not a theorem that performance cannot deteriorate; confident misclassification remains possible. The author demonstration study does not establish usability for a population of inexperienced users.
citation: Zizhao Wang, Xuesu Xiao , Bo Liu, Garrett Warnell, and Peter Stone. APPLI: Adaptive Planner Parameter Learning from Interventions . 2021 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA).
venue_full: 2021 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)

title: APPLR: Adaptive Planner Parameter Learning from Reinforcement
reading_depth: Full main text, PDF pp. 1–6, including meta-environment formulation, rewards, distributed training, test protocol, physical comparison, and limitations. References not close-read; no code replication.
problem: Static tuning and demonstration-based parameter libraries may be environment-specific and miss beneficial sequential decisions.
mechanism: Treat DWA and the world as a meta-environment and use TD3 to select eight planner parameters from sensing, local-goal direction, and previous parameters.
evidence_scope: 250 BARN training environments and 50 held-out tests, forty runs per method/environment; one physical course with five trials per method. Training uses five million transitions, about six hours on 500 actor CPUs.
writing_move: Make the learned action space the conceptual contribution, then separate training improvement, held-out transfer, parameter behavior, and physical deployment.
research_lesson: Explain the advantage and ceiling imposed by a retained classical planner, and report reward-induced trade-offs alongside faster traversal.
reviewer_question: Would a matched myopic parameter-selection baseline isolate sequential reasoning, and how do switching costs, smoothness rewards, and failure penalties change the ranking?

evidence_pages.observation: Parameters update every two seconds; simulated failures receive a 70-second score rather than a successful-traversal measurement.
Improvement diminishes in difficult environments; the authors conjecture a structural DWA performance ceiling, not a universal parameter-learning advantage.
Physical DWA time excludes its failed trial; APPLR is faster but less smooth than APPLD in confined spaces. The formulation currently assumes no parameter-switching cost.

limits_or_counterexample: Hardware success is a small one-course transfer test, not a general safety proof. Human-comparator data quality and available parameter flexibility differ, so the experiment does not isolate foresight as the sole causal explanation.
citation: Zifan Xu, Gauraang Dhamankar, Anirudh Nair, Xuesu Xiao , Garrett Warnell, Bo Liu, Zizhao Wang, and Peter Stone. APPLR: Adaptive Planner Parameter Learning from Reinforcement . 2021 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA).
venue_full: 2021 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)

title: Benchmarking Metric Ground Navigation
reading_depth: Main text on physical PDF pages 1–5 read in full; page 6 figure captions inspected; bibliography not close-read; no independent reanalysis of plots.
problem: Navigation methods lack a shared difficulty-controlled benchmark beyond ad hoc demonstration environments.
mechanism: Generate collision-reachable cellular-automaton worlds, compute five geometric path metrics, and learn a predictor of normalized traversal time.
evidence_scope: Three thousand simulated trials with DWA and E-Band define difficulty; fifty physical trials in five new worlds test correspondence.
writing_move: Connect a reproducibility gap to a reusable generator, explicit metrics, calibrated labels, and bounded physical validation.
research_lesson: A benchmark’s difficulty is relative to its robot, planners, parameter settings, and failure penalty; publish these alongside the map generator.
reviewer_question: Does the learned ranking transfer to other planner families or footprints, and how does withholding the prebuilt map only in physical tests affect validation?

evidence_pages.observation: Footprint inflation and flood fill reject unreachable worlds.
Two default-parameter planners, matched speed limits, and a 30-second failure penalty define training labels.
Five physical environments use no prebuilt map, unlike simulation.

limits_or_counterexample: Physical correspondence on five layouts does not establish algorithm-independent difficulty. Proposed curriculum and planning-cost uses are prospective, not evaluated here.
citation: Daniel Perille, Abigail Truong, Xuesu Xiao , and Peter Stone. Benchmarking Metric Ground Navigation . 2020 IEEE International Symposium on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics (SSRR).
venue_full: 2020 IEEE International Symposium on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics (SSRR)

title: Using Human-Inspired Signals to Disambiguate Navigational Intentions
reading_depth: Full main text on physical PDF pages 1–11 read; bibliography not close-read; tables read as extracted, no independent statistical reanalysis.
problem: Untrained pedestrians may misunderstand a robot’s intended passing direction, causing hallway conflicts.
mechanism: Translate a human gaze cue into a rendered robot head and compare first-exposure interpretation against LED turn signals.
evidence_scope: A 220-interaction human field study motivates a separate physical robot study; 27 of 38 recruited participants remain after exclusions.
writing_move: Move from a human phenomenon to a robot-specific hypothesis while explaining why the experiment measures cue interpretation rather than reaction to motion.
research_lesson: Prevent learning carryover when first-time legibility is the claim; explicitly report exclusions and the engineered conflict conditions.
reviewer_question: Would gaze retain its advantage with equal display salience, a no-cue control, less adversarial timing, and a population with different passing conventions?

evidence_pages.observation: The monitor is removed in the LED condition, changing more than the cue animation.
Each participant sees one cue once to avoid a teaching effect.
The robot deliberately turns left too late for motion-based reaction; 11 participants are excluded.
Gaze reduces conflict but still leaves half its trials in conflict; questionnaire differences are nonsignificant.

limits_or_counterexample: The result supports these implementations under first-exposure conditions, not a universal superiority of gaze or human-like embodiment.
citation: Justin Hart, Reuth Mirsky, Xuesu Xiao , Stone Tejeda, Bonny Mahajan, Jamin Goo, Kathryn Baldauf, Sydney Owen, and Peter Stone. Using Human-Inspired Signals to Disambiguate Navigational Intentions . 12th International Conference on Social Robotics (ICSR) 2020.
venue_full: 12th International Conference on Social Robotics (ICSR) 2020
research_line: Social navigation: data, benchmarks, and language reasoning

title: Benchmarking Tether-based UAV Motion Primitives
reading_depth: Full main text and figure captions on physical PDF pages 1–6 read; bibliography not close-read; plotted curves not independently digitized.
problem: Tethered UAVs need controllable three-dimensional motion, not merely station keeping or power delivery.
mechanism: Compare independent tether-coordinate position controllers with coupled inverse-Jacobian velocity control across waypoint densities.
evidence_scope: Thirty motion-capture trials on a bent path and fifteen position-control trials near the velocity controller’s singularity.
writing_move: An unexpected initial result leads to a second experiment that amplifies the hypothesized mechanism and exposes a measurement limitation.
research_lesson: When a tolerance masks the expected effect, redesign the experiment to discriminate explanations rather than treating a null result as confirmation.
reviewer_question: How robust are the controller comparisons to localization error, acceptance radius, gain tuning, and paths beyond the small test volume?

evidence_pages.observation: Catenary deformation is assumed corrected by an existing localizer.
Velocity control has a 90-degree elevation singularity; waypoint acceptance radius is 0.4 m.
Localization tolerance masks expected position-control error, motivating a second path.
A hybrid controller is suggested, not implemented and tested here.

limits_or_counterexample: Neither primitive is uniformly best. Denser waypoints can improve positional guidance while harming smoothness; velocity control must avoid singular configurations.
citation: Xuesu Xiao , Jan Dufek, and Robin Murphy. Benchmarking Tether-based UAV Motion Primitives . 2019 IEEE International Symposium on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics (SSRR).
venue_full: 2019 IEEE International Symposium on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics (SSRR)
research_line: Tethered UAV and risk-aware assistance (PhD era)

title: Explicit Motion Risk Representation
reading_depth: Full main text on physical PDF pages 1–6 read, including the concluding text after references in extraction order; formulas followed, not independently proved; bibliography not close-read.
problem: Low-dimensional path states omit action and traversal history that can affect mission failure.
mechanism: Define relative path-failure risk, formalize reachability and execution stability, and aggregate action-, state-, and path-dependent risk indices.
evidence_scope: Illustrative two-dimensional tethered-UAV path calculations use normalized factors with equal weights; physical validation is future work.
writing_move: Define the target quantity and its limits before formalizing its components, then use counterintuitive path comparisons to expose omitted factors.
research_lesson: Preserve distinctions across versions: this paper’s additive relative index is not the later risk paper’s noncompletion probability.
reviewer_question: What empirical evidence calibrates the weights and validates ordinal path rankings, and does the additive index preserve its intended ordering across discretizations?

evidence_pages.observation: The index provides relative ordering and explicitly does not support probability comparisons.
Non-negativity, monotonicity, and additivity are stipulated for the index.
Example factors are normalized and equally weighted.
Different robots and disturbances can reverse the illustrated path ranking; physical validation remains future work.

limits_or_counterexample: A formal representation is not a calibrated failure model. The safest illustrated path is not claimed to remain safest for every platform or mission.
citation: Xuesu Xiao , Jan Dufek, and Robin Murphy. Explicit Motion Risk Representation . 2019 IEEE International Symposium on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics (SSRR).
venue_full: 2019 IEEE International Symposium on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics (SSRR)
research_line: Tethered UAV and risk-aware assistance (PhD era)

title: Autonomous Visual Assistance for Robot Operations Using a Tethered UAV
reading_depth: Full main text and captions on physical PDF pages 1–13 read; bibliography not close-read; component equations not independently rederived.
problem: Remote robot operators lack useful external views, while a second manually operated camera robot adds coordination demands.
mechanism: Integrate viewpoint rewards, path-risk planning, tether localization, motion primitives, and contact planning into an aerial visual assistant.
evidence_scope: Indoor and disaster-prop demonstrations establish system feasibility; viewpoint study results and quantitative operator-performance evaluation remain outside this paper.
writing_move: Use a layered system description to connect human-facing motivation with planning, control, and hardware, then label deployment as proof of concept.
research_lesson: Declare autonomy precisely at each stage and preserve manual goal choices; integrating published components does not by itself establish the claimed human benefit.
reviewer_question: Does the assistant measurably improve task success, time, workload, or staffing when compared under equal operational conditions?

evidence_pages.observation: The professional-operator viewpoint study is ongoing and its results are reserved for another paper.
Viewpoints are manually specified; safety motivates withholding automatic goal selection.
The demonstrations are proof of concept; quantitative team and teleoperation measurements are future work.

limits_or_counterexample: Autonomous path execution is narrower than autonomous mission or viewpoint selection. Improved situational awareness is illustrated, not measured in a controlled user comparison.
citation: Xuesu Xiao , Jan Dufek, and Robin Murphy. Autonomous Visual Assistance for Robot Operations Using a Tethered UAV . 12th Conference on Field and Service Robotics (FSR) 2019.
venue_full: 12th Conference on Field and Service Robotics (FSR) 2019
research_line: Tethered UAV and risk-aware assistance (PhD era)

title: Motion Planning for a UAV with a Straight or Kinked Tether
reading_depth: Full main text and captions on physical PDF pages 1–7 read; bibliography not close-read; geometric algorithm not independently verified.
problem: A tether can block otherwise feasible UAV paths in cluttered three-dimensional environments.
mechanism: Either remove locations occluded from the tether reel or explicitly plan, stack, and relax obstacle contact points.
evidence_scope: Eighteen retained exploratory motion-capture trials after three exclusions compare reachability and path error on deliberately different navigation tasks.
writing_move: Frame the two methods as a reachability–accuracy trade-off, explain the shared executor, and disclose where the physical contact assumptions fail.
research_lesson: Report completion based on onboard feedback separately from ground-truth accuracy; a robot can declare success while substantially deviating from the plan.
reviewer_question: How does uncertain or moving contact geometry affect feasibility, and what criteria prevent tether damage or unsafe environmental contact?

evidence_pages.observation: Formed contact points are assumed fixed until relaxation.
The paper labels trials proof of concept, uses cardboard for safe contact, and reports excluded runs.
Contact-position error and slipping contacts accumulate; onboard completion does not imply precise execution.

limits_or_counterexample: Full free-space reachability is geometric and assumption-dependent. Contact permission is domain-specific, and the compared task sets are not identical.
citation: Xuesu Xiao , Jan Dufek, Mohamed Suhail, and Robin Murphy. Motion Planning for a UAV with a Straight or Kinked Tether . 2018 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS).
venue_full: 2018 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
research_line: Tethered UAV and risk-aware assistance (PhD era)

title: Estimating Achievable Range of Ground Robots Operating on Single Battery Discharge for Operational Efficacy Amelioration
reading_depth: Full main text and captions on physical PDF pages 1–8 read; bibliography not close-read; equations followed but not independently rederived.
problem: Battery lifetime alone does not reveal how far a ground robot can travel when propulsion and ancillary systems share energy.
mechanism: Build an analytical energy budget including terrain, duty cycle, losses, sensing, communication, and a battery-decay model.
evidence_scope: A custom small robot runs planar and fixed-slope trajectories with multiple duty cycles; wheels-up tests identify losses, while battery aging is simulated.
writing_move: State simplifying assumptions before derivation and separate identifiable component measurements from broader model ambitions.
research_lesson: Define whether maximum range uses a proven optimum or a chosen operating point, and distinguish calibrated system measurements from hypothetical component additions.
reviewer_question: Can the range estimate remain conservative when terrain, load, steering, onboard computation, or velocity changes beyond the calibration setup?

evidence_pages.observation: Terrain type and sensing frequency are fixed; onboard processing costs are excluded from the experiment.
The human-selected safe target velocity substitutes for an optimized velocity.
Battery aging is simulated and localization is disabled.
Encoder-only drift and slip limit range-estimation accuracy.

limits_or_counterexample: The tested energy composition is platform-specific. Resource accounting supports planning but does not demonstrate a safe return-to-base policy.
citation: Kshitij Tiwari , Xuesu Xiao , and Nak Young Chong. Estimating Achievable Range of Ground Robots Operating on Single Battery Discharge for Operational Efficacy Amelioration . 2018 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS).
venue_full: 2018 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)

title: Indoor UAV Localization Using a Tether
reading_depth: Full main text on physical PDF pages 1–5 read; page 6 figure captions inspected; bibliography not close-read; mechanics derivation not independently verified.
problem: Treating a suspended tether as perfectly straight biases UAV position estimates, especially as tether length increases.
mechanism: Estimate tension from the vehicle’s force balance and use a catenary model to correct elevation and effective tether length.
evidence_scope: Forty-eight hovering trials compare two localizers at 24 target locations in one azimuth plane, using motion capture averaged after stabilization.
writing_move: Explain a systematic error geometrically, derive a correction, and test the specific direction and tether-length dependence it predicts.
research_lesson: Separate sensor-estimation error from closed-loop target-tracking and hovering error; repeated samples within one hover are not independent experimental trials.
reviewer_question: How well does the model work during acceleration, wind, moving anchors, and contact, and what proportion of the reported error is controller rather than localization error?

evidence_pages.observation: The localizer assumes an unobstructed tether; contact planning is delegated to another work.
Vehicle lean comes from onboard IMU despite the emphasis on tether sensing.
Each target result averages 600 motion-capture samples over five seconds; azimuth error is not corrected.

limits_or_counterexample: The trial domain is quasi-static and geometrically restricted. The method avoids inertial integration, not all use of inertial sensing.
citation: Xuesu Xiao , Yiming Fan, Jan Dufek, and Robin Murphy. Indoor UAV Localization Using a Tether . 2018 IEEE International Symposium on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics (SSRR). Best Paper Finalist .
venue_full: 2018 IEEE International Symposium on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics (SSRR). Best Paper Finalist
research_line: Tethered UAV and risk-aware assistance (PhD era)

title: A Wearable System For Articulated Human Pose Tracking Under Uncertainty of Sensor Placement
reading_depth: Complete main text and figure/table captions, physical PDF pages 1–7; bibliography not close-read.
problem: Garment-mounted sensors violate the rigid sensor-to-body relationship assumed by conventional inertial pose trackers.
mechanism: The wearable prototype records synchronized inertial, proximity, and Kinect pose data; a kinematic baseline and reconstructed displacement expose motion-artifact structure.
evidence_scope: The laboratory dataset contains 215 trials from 12 subjects across five motion types. Only one IMU per segment enters the baseline; redundant IMUs and IR signals remain prospective resources.
writing_move: Make an unmet assumption experimentally visible before proposing a future algorithm: analyze errors by joint, time, speed, and cross-joint correlation.
research_lesson: A negative baseline result can support a dataset contribution when acquisition, calibration, and identifiable failure mechanisms are documented.
reviewer_question: How much apparent garment displacement arises from Kinect error, imperfect T-pose calibration, network delay, or the assumed stationary hat anchor?

evidence_pages.observation: The prototype is explicitly bulky, and processing synchronizes wireless sensor streams with optical measurements.
Upper-limb errors motivate examining calibration, sensor-movement latency, and changing displacement separately.
Displacement reconstruction uses optical joint angles and assumes the hat remains fixed to the head.
Data-driven tracking and more accurate optical references are future work, not demonstrated solutions.

limits_or_counterexample: Laboratory motion characterization does not establish unobtrusive long-term field tracking or prove learning will outperform a better-calibrated kinematic model.
citation: Xuesu Xiao and Shuayb Zarar. A Wearable System For Articulated Human Pose Tracking Under Uncertainty of Sensor Placement . 2018 IEEE International Conference on Biomedical Robotics and Biomechatronics (Biorob).
venue_full: 2018 IEEE International Conference on Biomedical Robotics and Biomechatronics (Biorob)

title: Machine Learning for Placement-insensitive Inertial Motion Capture
reading_depth: Complete main text, captions, and Table I on physical PDF pages 1–6; bibliography not close-read.
problem: Loose garment sensors introduce displacement, calibration, and latency errors that fixed-transform kinematics cannot absorb.
mechanism: Compare a hybrid DNN that estimates sensor displacement inside kinematics with an end-to-end DNN that predicts joint angles from temporally stacked sensor data.
evidence_scope: Training uses 215 laboratory trials from 12 subjects, plus a separate unseen-subject/motion test. The main split is 64/16/20 percent, without clearly specifying whether it is grouped by subject or trial.
writing_move: Explain two architectures through the particular error sources each can and cannot remove, then expose their generalization tradeoff.
research_lesson: Report both absolute out-of-distribution error and change from in-distribution performance; they answer different questions.
reviewer_question: Does the split prevent correlated-frame leakage, and does the hybrid's smaller degradation justify its higher absolute unseen error?

evidence_pages.observation: Displacement labels inherit sensor-fusion assumptions; direct labels come from optical joint estimates.
Redundant IMUs improve performance; the best tested model excludes IR sensors.
Hybrid RMSE changes 16.42° to 14.54°; direct estimation changes 6.14° to 10.17° on unseen data.

limits_or_counterexample: The hybrid degrades less but remains less accurate on this unseen set. Correlated training/validation curves alone do not establish absence of overfitting or leakage.
citation: Xuesu Xiao and Shuayb Zarar. Machine Learning for Placement-insensitive Inertial Motion Capture . 2018 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA).
venue_full: 2018 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)

title: Packet Loss Concealment with Recurrent Neural Networks for Wireless Inertial Pose Tracking
reading_depth: Complete main text and captions, physical PDF pages 1–5; page 4 Table II also visually verified. Bibliography not close-read.
problem: Missing wireless IMU packets disrupt downstream pose estimates even when the physical motion is smooth.
mechanism: LSTMs predict missing samples; correlation-based sensor clustering trades separate predictors for vectorized multichannel inference.
evidence_scope: Experiments inject Bernoulli and Gilbert losses into recorded motion data, fix Gilbert q at 0.8, and evaluate four loss rates and eleven grouping configurations.
writing_move: Connect a networking defect to the application metric, reporting both signal reconstruction error and joint-angle error.
research_lesson: An intermediate improvement must be checked against the downstream non-degraded reference, not just against a damaged baseline.
reviewer_question: What definition supports the abstract's full concealment through 20% loss, given residual tracking degradation in Table II?

evidence_pages.observation: A single network for all channels did not converge in the reported experiments; correlation grouping motivates the alternative.
At 20% loss, errors are 20.4° and 21.3°, compared with 18.1° without loss.
Baseline-equivalent tracking is described near 10% loss; grouping has a nonmonotonic effect.

limits_or_counterexample: Synthetic fixed-burst losses do not establish robustness to arbitrary field outages. Group-count arguments are not measured end-to-end latency on a constrained deployment processor.
citation: Xuesu Xiao and Shuayb Zarar. Packet Loss Concealment with Recurrent Neural Networks for Wireless Inertial Pose Tracking . 2018 IEEE International Conference on Wearable and Implantable Body Sensor Networks (BSN).
venue_full: 2018 IEEE International Conference on Wearable and Implantable Body Sensor Networks (BSN)

title: Visual Servoing for Teleoperation using a Tethered UAV
reading_depth: Complete main text and captions, physical PDF pages 1–6; bibliography not close-read.
problem: A teleoperator needs informative third-person views without manually coordinating another camera robot.
mechanism: AprilTag pose estimates and homogeneous transformations define the desired tethered-UAV/camera configuration, followed by decoupled control of available motion variables.
evidence_scope: An obstacle-free indoor experiment moves the marker through the workspace while the tether ground station is detached from the PackBot. Reported pose errors characterize servoing, not operator task performance.
writing_move: Derive the controller from explicit coordinate frames and transformations, then separate achieved component capability from the system research agenda.
research_lesson: Distinguish observing a state dimension from actively controlling it and distinguish stable tracking from useful viewpoint selection.
reviewer_question: Which rotational dimensions are actually controlled, and how do marker occlusion, moving-base dynamics, and obstacle avoidance affect the demonstrated tracking?

evidence_pages.observation: Although roll is tracked, the gimbal roll is deliberately not controlled to preserve upright video.
The ground station is dismounted and tests omit obstacles.
Optimal viewpoints, risk-aware obstacle avoidance, and task-dependent targets remain unresolved.

limits_or_counterexample: The six-dimensional pose description does not imply active six-axis correction. Reduced staffing, improved awareness, and task efficiency are motivations or prospects, not tested human outcomes.
citation: Xuesu Xiao , Jan Dufek, and Robin Murphy. Visual Servoing for Teleoperation using a Tethered UAV . 2017 IEEE International Symposium on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics (SSRR).
venue_full: 2017 IEEE International Symposium on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics (SSRR)
research_line: Tethered UAV and risk-aware assistance (PhD era)

title: Visual Pose Stabilization of Tethered Small Unmanned Aerial System to Assist Drowning Victim Recovery
reading_depth: Complete main text and captions, physical PDF pages 1–7; bibliography not close-read.
problem: Tether-relative stabilization lets a camera UAV drift with its ground station, disturbing image-based rescue-robot control.
mechanism: Track image features, recover rotation and translation direction from essential geometry, and threshold visual displacement before converting corrections to tether commands.
evidence_scope: Nine stabilized and three unstabilized indoor trials move the ground station along separate axes. Floor markers and two external videos approximate ground truth; outdoor wind and downstream USV benefit are not tested.
writing_move: Explain why the application's oblique view breaks a planar assumption, then document the replacement method's own degeneracy.
research_lesson: A component experiment should isolate its intended disturbance while retaining a separate integration test for the ultimate application.
reviewer_question: How do feature loss, coplanar water scenes, moving background objects, and reference resets affect long-term world-frame position error?

evidence_pages.observation: The epipolar approach permits noncoplanar features but is degenerate when features are coplanar.
Feature depletion resets the reference; monocular translation has direction but no scale.
The reported aggregate displacement is 34 cm with stabilization, versus 98 cm without, at approximately 4.85 Hz.
Outdoor wind, explicit orientation evaluation, and integration benefits remain future tests.

limits_or_counterexample: Indoor moving-cart results do not establish coastal rescue robustness, and resetting the reference can stop further drift without recovering the original pose.
citation: Jan Dufek, Xuesu Xiao , and Robin Murphy. Visual Pose Stabilization of Tethered Small Unmanned Aerial System to Assist Drowning Victim Recovery . 2017 IEEE International Symposium on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics (SSRR).
venue_full: 2017 IEEE International Symposium on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics (SSRR)
research_line: Tethered UAV and risk-aware assistance (PhD era)

title: UAV Assisted USV Visual Navigation for Marine Mass Casualty Incident Response
reading_depth: Complete main text and captions, physical PDF pages 1–6; bibliography not close-read.
problem: Shore-level perspective obscures the relative positions of a rescue USV and distant victims.
mechanism: An aerial camera supplies image-frame tracking, motion-history heading estimates, optional perspective rectification, and line-of-sight/PID USV commands with approach deceleration.
evidence_scope: Thirty visual-navigation runs across four outdoor sites reach selected targets. GPS supplies evaluation coordinates, not victim-location input; operators initialize the visual tracker and select targets.
writing_move: Begin with a concrete field-perception failure, justify simple adequate components, and report environmental conditions alongside navigation results.
research_lesson: System novelty can lie in task-enabling integration and deployment evidence rather than replacing every classical algorithm.
reviewer_question: How are safe victim approach, moving targets, tracker loss, and operator intervention defined, and how does performance compare with manual control?

evidence_pages.observation: The paper explicitly accepts histogram tracking as sufficient for these trials rather than requiring more sophisticated perception.
GPS evaluates trajectories; a quantified comparison with human operators is deferred.
The four sites contribute 1, 14, 11, and 4 runs, with substantial variation in wind and cross-track error.

limits_or_counterexample: Successful target-reaching is not a clinical rescue-outcome study. Unequal site sample sizes and differing conditions limit cross-site causal conclusions and claims of general plug-and-play compatibility.
citation: Xuesu Xiao , Jan Dufek, and Robin Murphy. UAV Assisted USV Visual Navigation for Marine Mass Casualty Incident Response . 2017 IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS).
venue_full: 2017 IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
research_line: Tethered UAV and risk-aware assistance (PhD era)

title: Two Case Studies and Gaps Analysis of Flood Assessment for Emergency Management with Small Unmanned Aerial Systems
reading_depth: Complete main text and captions, physical PDF pages 1–8; Figure 1 on page 2 visually checked because its extracted flight table was corrupted. Bibliography not close-read.
problem: Useful aerial flood imagery does not automatically become timely information for emergency-management decisions.
mechanism: Two operational case studies trace missions, staffing, data products, availability delays, and adoption gaps across the data-to-decision process.
evidence_scope: Twenty-one flights at seventeen locations during two 2016 floods generate 129 GB of raw and processed data; twenty flights are manually directed by county experts.
writing_move: Structure the contribution around who needs which information when, rather than treating successful flight as the final outcome.
research_lesson: Include transport, curation, interpretation, and personnel costs in the experimental system boundary.
reviewer_question: Which recommendations are observed operational facts, expert interpretations, or untested cost-benefit hypotheses, and how might other agencies differ?

evidence_pages.observation: Immediate field video contrasts with a two-to-six-hour delay for high-resolution transfer to the emergency operations center.
Remote presence suited four of five flown mission types; comprehensive photogrammetric products were not the primary demand.
Expert placement and data-manager staffing have unresolved opportunity costs; formal ROI analysis is absent.

limits_or_counterexample: More autonomy or more data is not necessarily more useful. These are context-rich cases from one county, not a controlled comparison proving a universally optimal workflow or commercial tool.
citation: Robin Murphy, Jan Dufek, Traci Sarmiento, Grant Wilde, Xuesu Xiao , Richard Smith, Sam Allred, Adam Wright, Jeff Braun, Lachlan Mullen, Justin Adams, and Jess Gingrich. Two Case Studies and Gaps Analysis of Flood Assessment for Emergency Management with Small Unmanned Aerial Systems . 2016 IEEE International Symposium on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics (SSRR).

title: Locomotive Reduction for Snake Robots
reading_depth: Complete main text and captions, physical PDF pages 1–6; bibliography not close-read.
problem: Direct navigation control of a sixteen-joint snake robot is complicated by internal shape changes and ambiguous body heading.
mechanism: A virtual chassis and continuously varied conical-sidewinding taper expose a differential-drive-like interface; a finite-state controller switches turning, reversal, rolling, and climbing modes.
evidence_scope: A camera-instrumented indoor demonstration follows deliberately chosen waypoints and transitions to pole climbing. It establishes integration feasibility, without a repeated-trial error or baseline comparison.
writing_move: Introduce an intuitive low-dimensional interface before deriving its gait-level implementation and showing the capability it preserves.
research_lesson: A useful abstraction should simplify common operations while retaining an explicit route to specialized behavior.
reviewer_question: Under what surfaces, speeds, shapes, and tracking errors does the gait-to-curvature mapping approximate the claimed vehicle model?

evidence_pages.observation: Conical taper relates to curvature through a coefficient calibrated for different snakes and skins.
The controller assumes constant linear speed and absorbs proportional factors into a tuned gain.
Waypoints are hand-picked to exercise transitions; a body-length-diameter circle simplifies collision planning.

limits_or_counterexample: A differential-drive-like interface does not transfer all guarantees automatically. The conservative circular footprint and overhead fiducials limit the showcased navigation setting, even though specialized gaits remain available.
citation: Xuesu Xiao , Ellen Cappo, Weikun Zhen, Jin Dai, Ke Sun, Chaohui Gong, Matthew J. Travers, and Howie Choset. Locomotive Reduction for Snake Robots . 2015 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA).

title: A Study on Learning Social Robot Navigation with Multimodal Perception
reading_depth: Complete main text and captions, physical PDF pages 1–6; reference-only pages 7–8 not close-read.
problem: Social navigation decisions may need both geometric structure from LiDAR and semantic cues from images.
mechanism: Behavior cloning compares image, voxelized point-cloud, and fused inputs for short waypoint sequences and current velocity commands.
evidence_scope: The study uses eighteen training and eight test SCAND trials, three training runs, and eight human participants in curated encounters. RGB-only control is excluded from the human comparison after unsafe close approaches.
writing_move: Evaluate both imitation loss and human-perceived interaction quality rather than treating them as interchangeable.
research_lesson: A positive offline result needs a separately stated human-study conclusion, including null differences and safety exclusions.
reviewer_question: Why does the conclusion assert clear large-margin human-study superiority when the reported comparison with point-cloud-only shows no significant advantage?

evidence_pages.observation: The supplied goal is only 2.5 m ahead on demonstration odometry; history length is fixed at one.
The actual training/testing subset is eighteen/eight trials.
The human study reports no significant multimodal advantage over LiDAR-only, while concluding broader superiority.

limits_or_counterexample: Demonstration-matching error is not a complete social-compliance measure. Curated one- and two-person encounters do not establish dense-crowd or long-term deployment safety, and the human study cannot compare the excluded RGB policy.
citation: Bhabaranjan Panigrahi, Amir Hossain Raj, Mohammad Nazeri, and Xuesu Xiao . A Study on Learning Social Robot Navigation with Multimodal Perception . 14th Workshop on Planning, Perception and Navigation for Intelligent Vehicles @IROS 2024.

title: Learning Real-world Autonomous Navigation by Self-Supervised Environment Synthesis
reading_depth: Complete main text and captions, physical PDF pages 1–6; reference-only page 7 not close-read.
problem: Policies trained in artificial maps may repeatedly struggle with obstacle configurations encountered during deployment.
mechanism: Segment deployment trajectories, retain difficult scenarios using a recovery-behavior proxy, synthesize a compact training set, and fine-tune an adaptive classical-planner parameter policy.
evidence_scope: Large-scale evaluation uses simulated Matterport homes explicitly as a real-world surrogate, with five held-out homes. Physical testing fine-tunes on two reconstructed challenging scenarios and reports five repetitions per policy.
writing_move: Isolate environmental distribution mismatch from sensor and dynamics mismatch, and identify exactly which part the method addresses.
research_lesson: Separate the full synthesis pipeline's evidence from a smaller physical demonstration that omits its generative component.
reviewer_question: How sensitive are gains to the backward-command difficulty proxy, threshold, synthesis budget, and failures omitted from the time-cost mean?

evidence_pages.observation: More than fifty negative-velocity commands marks a challenging scenario, tying difficulty to the deployed planner.
Five thousand simulated deployments yield 3,769 difficult scenarios; GAN synthesis produces one hundred training environments.
The physical study directly reconstructs two scenarios instead of using GAN synthesis; time metrics concern successful trials in the simulator evaluation.

limits_or_counterexample: This is not large-scale physical deployment evidence. Random sampling does not improve success over the original policy in Table I, so collecting relevant data alone is insufficient.
citation: Zifan Xu, Anirudh Nair, Xuesu Xiao , and Peter Stone. Learning Real-world Autonomous Navigation by Self-Supervised Environment Synthesis . First Workshop on Photorealistic Image and Environment Synthesis for Robotics (PIES-Rob) @IROS 2023.

title: A Protocol for Validating Social Navigation Policies
reading_depth: Complete main text and captions, physical PDF pages 1–4; Tables I–V on pages 3–4 visually checked. Reference-only page 5 not close-read.
problem: Social-navigation policies need comparable evaluation that captures participants' lived experience without losing all repeatability.
mechanism: Five canonical encounters combine lightweight scenario instructions with immediate, scenario-specific Likert questionnaires and reverse-coded negative items.
evidence_scope: Pilot tests repeat scenarios in two building locations, compare participants and times, and contrast MPC with demonstration-augmented control. These are initial measurement studies, not broad cross-laboratory psychometric validation.
writing_move: Make the evaluation protocol itself reproducible through scenario definitions, question wording, timing, and explicit failure examples.
research_lesson: Use first-person reports to complement external observation, while separately validating the instrument's coding and reliability.
reviewer_question: How are zero/cannot-tell responses and positively worded item 17 handled, and which reliability statistic supports the similarity-of-means argument?

evidence_pages.observation: Item 17 is positively worded but marked for reverse coding; zero means cannot tell or something went wrong.
Three-person and repeated-single-person comparisons infer reliability from similar descriptive averages.
A robot contacting a participant's foot elicited a negative in-situ report despite being visually subtle.

limits_or_counterexample: Repeated trials from one person are not independent participant diversity. A favorable mean questionnaire score cannot substitute for collision accounting or authorize deliberately unsafe encounters.
citation: Sören Pirk, Edward Lee, Xuesu Xiao , Leila Takayama, Anthony Francis, and Alexander Toshev. A Protocol for Validating Social Navigation Policies . Social Robot Navigation: Advances and Evaluation @ICRA 2022.

title: Task-Independent Causal State Abstraction
reading_depth: Complete main text on physical PDF pages 1–4 and complete appendices on pages 7–10; reference-only pages 5–6 not close-read. No independent theorem or code reproduction.
problem: Dense learned dynamics and reward predictors can use irrelevant correlations, impairing transfer and sample efficiency.
mechanism: Learn sparse dynamics dependencies, classify controllable and action-relevant variables, omit action-irrelevant variables, and plan with an abstract-state reward predictor.
evidence_scope: One simulated manipulation environment tests reaching and grasping; distribution shifts move non-interactable markers. Scripted exploration supplies dynamics data and occasional downstream demonstrations.
writing_move: Define the abstraction precisely, then design separate baselines to distinguish dynamics sparsity from reward-state abstraction.
research_lesson: Attach the admissible task class and shift type to every broad transfer claim; inspect appendices for essential training assistance.
reviewer_question: Does the learned graph remain reliable under less scripted exploration, latent confounding, interacting distractors, or rewards depending on omitted variables?

evidence_pages.observation: The abstraction retains controllable variables and their action-relevant ancestors.
Task independence excludes rewards depending on action-irrelevant variables.
Variable-level graphs are imperfect; downstream episodes use scripted demonstrations with ten-percent probability, and vanilla MBRL wins in-distribution grasping reward.

limits_or_counterexample: Sparse predictive dependence is only loosely termed causal here. Robustness to displaced irrelevant markers does not establish arbitrary causal identification, task universality, or universal performance superiority.
citation: Zizhao Wang, Xuesu Xiao , and Peter Stone. Task-Independent Causal State Abstraction . 4th Robot Learning Workshop: Self-Supervised and Lifelong Learning @NeurIPS 2021.
venue_full: 4th Robot Learning Workshop: Self-Supervised and Lifelong Learning @NeurIPS 2021

title: How Compound-Wave Control Alleviates Hyper-Redundant Control Complexity
reading_depth: Complete one-page extended abstract read; no independent visual or experimental verification.
problem: Hyper-redundant snake control is hard to express at the task level despite the mechanism's locomotor versatility.
mechanism: Connects compound serpenoid robot controls with biological low-dimensional control templates and extends the analogy to three-dimensional turning behaviors.
evidence_scope: A short conceptual synthesis with figure-based biological/robot turning demonstrations and links to locomotive reduction; no full statistical evaluation is supplied.
writing_move: Builds a two-way bridge: robotics provides testable low-dimensional hypotheses for biology, while biological behavior suggests robot control parameters.
research_lesson: A cross-disciplinary analogy is productive when it yields variables and experiments, not merely an evocative resemblance.
reviewer_question: Which aspects are demonstrated mechanical behaviors, and which remain hypotheses about how biological snakes actually control themselves?

evidence_pages.observation: Distinguishes compound-wave templates, robot implementation, and proposed biological investigation.

limits_or_counterexample: A robot reproducing a behavior does not prove the animal uses the same control law; an extended abstract has a narrower evidentiary burden than a full experimental paper.
citation: Xuesu Xiao , Henry Astley, Jin Dai, Weikun Zhen, Chaohui Gong, Daniel Goldman, and Howie Choset. How Compound-Wave Control Alleviates Hyper-Redundant Control Complexity . Workshop on Robotics-inspired Biology @ICRA 2015.
venue_full: Workshop on Robotics-inspired Biology @ICRA 2015

title: Extended Abstract: Using Parallelized Containers for Reinforcement Learning on Large Computer Clusters
reading_depth: Complete two-page main text read; reference list not close-read; historical software details not tested.
problem: Robotics RL requires parallel simulation even when a shared compute cluster lacks the task's software stack.
mechanism: Packages actors in Singularity containers and coordinates experience/policy exchange with a host-side learner using bound shared folders and HTCondor scheduling.
evidence_scope: An implementation-oriented extended abstract with algorithms and an APPLR/Gazebo example; it does not present a large scaling benchmark.
writing_move: Writes the infrastructure as reusable interfaces and minimal algorithms, with a concrete project showing how to instantiate them.
research_lesson: Reproducibility can be a research-enabling contribution: define data persistence, task packaging, and orchestration contracts explicitly.
reviewer_question: How are concurrent writes, stale policies, failures, deterministic seeds, and throughput handled beyond the conceptual shared-folder design?

evidence_pages.observation: Specifies shared actor/learner buffer and policy exchange.
Explains cluster-specific scheduler/container constraints and provides implementation pointers.

limits_or_counterexample: These are historical deployment choices, not current installation instructions or proof that containers alone ensure deterministic reproducibility.

title: Energy Utilization and Energetic Estimation of Achievable Range for Wheeled Mobile Robots Operating on a Single Battery Discharge
reading_depth: All six main-text pages read; reference list not close-read; plots not independently digitized.
problem: Travel range depends on mission-time ancillary loads and drive-chain losses, not simply battery energy divided by rolling work.
mechanism: Extends an ideal terramechanics model with duty cycle, velocity, battery mass fraction, and a chain of efficiencies; calibrates losses with wheels-up and field tests.
evidence_scope: KK2 propulsion experiments deliberately isolate steering/robotics power; several battery-load configurations test range predictions.
writing_move: Starts with a tractable ideal equation, enumerates violated assumptions, then exposes the measurements needed to correct it.
research_lesson: A model should make its calibration experiment derivable; isolate components to identify parameters, but narrow validation claims accordingly.
reviewer_question: Do efficiency assumptions survive changed load/terrain, and which reported ranges are actually traversed versus extrapolated?

evidence_pages.observation: Separate ancillary power makes propulsion-branch efficiency one during validation.
The eighteen-battery case uses equivalent weight and multiplies a one-battery traverse.

limits_or_counterexample: Faster travel saves time-dependent energy only within model/operating assumptions; this is not advice to drive arbitrarily fast or ignore mission sensing.
citation: Xuesu Xiao and William L. "Red" Whittaker. Energy Utilization and Energetic Estimation of Achievable Range for Wheeled Mobile Robots Operating on a Single Battery Discharge . tech. report CMU-RI-TR-14-15, Robotics Institute, Carnegie Mellon University, June, 2015.

title: Exploration of Planetary Skylights and Tunnels
reading_depth: Complete argument-level reading of substantive main-report chapters 3–14, physical PDF pp9–159, plus front matter pp1–8 and acknowledgements on p159. All displayed source text and captions in that scope were read; selected central visuals were separately inspected. This is not a proof, code, raw-data, or exhaustive figure reproduction.
problem: Orbital observations cannot resolve pit interiors; access, sensing, energy, communications, and scientific value impose coupled mission constraints.
mechanism: A multi-author NIAC report connects target taxonomy and robot roles to mission templates, configuration trade studies, modeling algorithms, terrestrial prototypes, and a technology roadmap.
evidence_scope: Complete main-report reading covers orbital-data reconstructions, simulated flyover, analog field tests, calibration, visualization, recharge, terrain classification, and modeled energetics. These heterogeneous results are not a planetary mission demonstration.
writing_move: Make a long program legible through objectives, role decomposition, candidate rejection, instrument-specific tests, explicit assumptions, and remaining dependencies.
research_lesson: Measure the mission-relevant bottleneck and preserve evidence type: reconstructed appearance, calibrated geometry, classification, autonomous control, and deployment readiness are different claims.
reviewer_question: Which claim rests on measured trials, reference-assisted alignment, a proxy, a restricted subset, borrowed prior results, an analytic projection, or a proposed future capability?

evidence_pages.observation: The report orders orbital, flyover, surface, descent, and subsurface exploration as information-generating stages that inform later mission design.
Ramp geometry, cave access, latitude, and depth/diameter affect robot and sensing choices; detecting a void does not establish its accessibility.
Descent, scientific exploration, infrastructure emplacement, and a power/communications link are distinct roles; one platform can fulfill several.
The dropped sensor pod obtains only seconds of imagery with motion blur and limited viewpoint control, undermining Cavehopper's modeling role despite its access potential.
Tyrolean and scree-slope configurations are retained; other concepts are rejected for combinations of control, sensing, tether, debris, power, and landing risks.

The weighted selection matrix reports Rock Crawler 174 and Rocker-Bogie 167; their sums were independently recomputed from the displayed rows. These are assigned decision scores, not measured performance differences.
The proposed mission branches on ramp availability; a no-ramp case uses a Tyrolean system to model, deploy a crawler, and support return for recharge and data transfer.
Low reflectance at the chosen LIDAR wavelength reduces practical range; nominal manufacturer range must be adjusted for the intended material.

The 40-fold density and up-to-40% range-accuracy figures are attributed to Wong's earlier work on some lunar analogs, with optical dependence; they are not universal new measurements from every report experiment.
The local surface estimate prioritizes high-frequency detail rather than correct gross geometry; the separate MRF fusion pass anchors global consistency using range data.
A single height-like representation distorts strongly three-dimensional pits; planarity testing and recursive local partitioning adapt the representation to concavities.
The 5m/pixel DEM is compared with a much coarser WAC reference; most discrepancies fall within roughly ±50m after ICP, not a verified worst-case bound below 50m.
Shadowed regions remain poorly modeled; a moving shadow boundary is offered as a possible false stereo correspondence, not a confirmed physical floor discontinuity.
The illustrated flyover uses simulated LIDAR and imagery. Trajectory/view optimization was not attempted, and wall coverage remains limited by oblique viewing geometry.
The planning formulation combines a coarse pit model, surface patches, time-varying illumination, feasible viewpoints, and rover motion limits to select where and when to image.

The feasibility dataset comprises 205 camera views from 14 tripod stations over less than 1.5 hours on an overcast day; it simulates rover viewpoints rather than demonstrating autonomous view planning.

Camera geometry is manually scaled/aligned, cropped, and refined with reference-based ICP. Reported mean distance is 0.042m, standard deviation 0.16m, maximum 8.1m; viewpoint coverage and reference gaps affect interpretation.

White reference points and error-colored reconstruction points show unequal spatial coverage. A localized apparent-error patch coincides with sparse or missing reference coverage; the caption identifies this as a likely explanation.
HDR is compared with LDR through a local image-contrast metric; that metric alone is not an observer-task or scientific-decision evaluation.
Two scan patterns are tested with total-station payload tracking. Horizontal stripes appear smoother in preliminary analysis; pendulum effects and reduced lunar atmospheric damping qualify transfer.
Rotary-scanner overlap provides a calibration constraint. Ego-motion correction and calibration are explicit prerequisites to interpreting the reconstructed geometry.

Combined, aligned, downsampled Tyrobot models yield reported mean/median nearest-reference distances of 0.47/0.31m. Figure 95 removes some outliers for display; this is not a raw odometric localization guarantee.

Density counts ignore voxels with fewer than five points; mean 5170 versus median 773 points per retained 1m voxel exposes uneven sampling, not complete coverage of an independently defined target surface.

Pluto's Cave camera-only reconstructions are explicitly qualitative because no ground-truth shape exists. Robot-mounted camera evaluation at Indian Tunnel instead uses scaled, cropped, ICP-aligned reference comparisons.

Most reconstructed camera points are reported within 0.15m only after scale is set from ground truth. Flash LIDAR trades simultaneous acquisition and small size against low resolution, power, and noise.

Rigid registration protects metric geometry but retains artifacts; optional planar/affine alignment improves visible detail while the text explicitly warns that features may no longer be metrically accurate.
Three viewpoints, controlled illumination, HDR, and LIDAR jointly estimate local surface normals and albedo; MRF fusion wraps detail around the measured base geometry.
Poisson reconstruction creates a spurious domed cap when making the mesh watertight; manual trimming and outlier removal are disclosed.
Figure 120 illustrates an appearance enhancement. The text motivates user understanding, but the demonstration is not a measured human-performance comparison.

Candidate illumination composites are selected by a multiscale contrast score. The optimization target is image contrast, with viewpoint and reflectance assumptions, rather than proven scientific-task benefit.
A 3D-printed pit preserves a central hole due to missing LIDAR returns instead of filling it for aesthetics; anaglyph display is presented as an accessible output medium.
Adjustable pulley geometry and component mounting support field-driven parameter changes without expensive refabrication.
Bench pull tests vary pulley and line parameters to estimate friction; the taut-line ideal is balanced against practical tension and payload sag.
A hobby-rocket mechanism demonstrates deployment across 34m on Earth; lunar range advantages and full rover-assisted anchoring are mission extrapolations, not completed planetary tests.

Connection succeeds in 40/64 trials across 16 orientations (62.5%). Restricting misalignment, pitch-down, and contamination leaves 31/31 successes; induction/conduction redundancy adds little observed reliability.
The 870nm LIDAR works well only substantially inside its quoted 30m range on dark coal-like surfaces, connecting field material response back to sensing and viewpoint design.

Human-controlled slope trials vary rock material, trajectory, and power. Larger rocks introduce bouncing and smooth large rocks introduce slip; these are not autonomous terrain-adaptive control demonstrations.

The report records 80,000 six-channel IMU samples at about 2ms intervals, a 40,000/40,000 train/test division, and 100-sample moving windows. Trajectory independence and partition order require clarification.
ANN, PCA/1NN, and several SVM kernels/features are searched; the report gives best accuracies but does not clearly establish a separate model-selection set.

The best four-class result is 70.25%; merging same-size contour classes changes the task and produces 81%. The figure displays ordered test outcomes, not a confusion matrix; class-name wording differs from p137.

Energy/range curves are analytical scenarios for a 10kg rover, assumed 30W ancillary power, duty cycle, and battery energy. They predict reduced time-based overhead at higher speed; they are not measured long-foray results.

The roadmap distinguishes baseline and extended capabilities across Scout/Wayfarer, Spelunker, and human missions. Its 2015–2050 timeline is a 2014 planning forecast, not an achieved deployment record.
Terrain sensing is preliminary; reliable scree and bouldering autonomy, appropriate control, and anomaly recovery explicitly require additional development.
The report identifies user-response evaluation and mission-specific interface tailoring as further work, bounding earlier claims about enhanced understanding.
Terrestrial rubber wheels and dynamic suspensions do not transfer unchanged to vacuum and thermal extremes; environmental qualification is a separate readiness dependency.

The report attributes major Lumenhancement work to Wong and view-planning research to Jones. An unfunded mission proposal is described as useful for forcing program alignment, not as a successful mission.
A proposal that was not selected nevertheless helped build interdisciplinary understanding; this is program-development impact rather than experimental performance evidence.

The conclusion contrasts potentially useful minimalist reconnaissance with substantial development still needed for deep-cave access; strong mission rhetoric should be read with the chapter-level evidence limits.

limits_or_counterexample: Forty of 64 recharge trials succeeded overall; 31/31 is a restricted subset. Ground-truth alignment limits mapping claims. Classification changes classes at 81%; split independence is unclear, not proven invalid. Visualization gains lack direct user-task validation. Historical mission forecasts are not current status.

Whittaker, Steve McGuire, Xuesu Xiao , Rick Shanor, Ander Solorzano, Tom Carlone, Wennie Tabib, Christopher Greve, Lauren Schneider, Nathan Otten, and William L. "Red" Whittaker. Exploration of Planetary Skylights and Tunnels . NASA Technical Report, 2014.
venue_full: NASA Technical Report, 2014

title: Energy Considerations for Wheeled Mobile Robots Operating on a Single Battery Discharge
reading_depth: Full main text on PDF pages 7–26 read, plus front matter 1–6; references p27 not close-read. Original PDF p25 rendered and visually checked.
problem: An ideal battery-to-range estimate omits ancillary energy, internal losses, and the mass cost of carrying more batteries.
mechanism: Develops an energy-chain model, derives range and cost-of-transport relationships, and calibrates propulsion efficiencies on KK2.
evidence_scope: Wheels-up/athletic-track experiments with isolated ancillary power, followed by battery-load estimates; the eighteen-battery value is a disclosed extrapolation.
writing_move: Uses the report format to retain derivations, instrumentation, assumptions, and experimental limitations behind the shorter later paper.
research_lesson: Keep a long-form reproducibility trail, distinguish measurement from extrapolation, and reconcile every table label against equations.
reviewer_question: Are units and cost-of-transport values internally consistent, and does validation include the variable ancillary consumption emphasized by the motivation?

evidence_pages.observation: Visually verified extrapolation disclosure; table heading says C=2.4 while equation/text say C=0.25.
Requires terrain resistance and ancillary-consumption estimates.

limits_or_counterexample: A valuable paper can contain an apparent consistency error. Treat the mismatch as an item to resolve, not evidence to invent a corrected value or dismiss the whole study.
